section: Germany: non-residents with German income, and foreign tax credits, tax year 2026
wording: This skill decides whether a person is taxed in Germany on worldwide income or only on German income, then works out how the German income is taxed: by assessment, by wage tax, or by a flat withholding. It also covers the reverse case: a German resident with foreign income who wants credit for the foreign tax.

section: Who this applies to
wording: **Unlimited liability (§ 1(1) EStG).** A person with a residence (Wohnsitz) or habitual abode (gewöhnlicher Aufenthalt) in Germany is taxed on worldwide income.

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Residence (§ 8 AO):** a home the person keeps and uses, in circumstances showing they will keep and use it. A flat kept available in Germany is enough, even if the person spends most of the year abroad.

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Habitual abode (§ 9 AO):** staying in a way that shows the stay is not just temporary. A continuous stay of more than six months always counts, from the first day; short breaks are ignored. The six-month rule does not apply to a purely private stay (visit, holiday, cure) of up to one year (§ 9 sentence 3 AO).

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **German state employees abroad (§ 1(2) EStG):** German nationals paid from a German public purse, taxed abroad only like non-residents, stay fully liable.

section: Who this applies to
wording: **Limited liability (§ 1(4) EStG).** A person with neither residence nor habitual abode in Germany is taxed only on German-source income listed in § 49 EStG.

section: Who this applies to
wording: **The § 1(3) option.** A non-resident can apply to be treated as fully liable for their German income if, in the calendar year, either:

section: Who this applies to
wording: - at least 90% of their total income is subject to German income tax, or

section: Who this applies to
wording: - the income not subject to German tax is no more than the Grundfreibetrag, EUR 12,348 for 2026. The amount is cut to ¾, ½ or ¼ for residents of lower-cost countries (BMF country groups; Austria and most of Western Europe are in group 1, full amount).

section: Who this applies to
wording: German income that a tax treaty limits to a reduced rate (for example dividends) counts as not subject to German tax for the test (§ 1(3) sentence 3). The foreign income must be shown by a certificate from the foreign tax authority (§ 1(3) sentence 5). § 50a withholding still applies (§ 1(3) sentence 6).

section: Who this applies to
wording: **§ 1a EStG, EU/EEA nationals.** An EU or EEA national who is fully liable under § 1(1) or treated so under § 1(3) can have a spouse who lives in another EU/EEA state treated as fully liable, so the couple gets joint assessment and splitting. For the § 1(3) test the income of both spouses counts and the Grundfreibetrag is doubled to EUR 24,696 (§ 1a(1) no. 2). A non-EU/EEA national under § 1(3) gets the Grundfreibetrag but not splitting.

section: Who this applies to
wording: **Companies.** A company with neither its seat nor its place of management in Germany has limited corporate tax liability on its German income (§ 2 no. 1 KStG). Income settled by withholding is final unless it belongs to a German business (§ 32(1) KStG). A German permanent establishment is assessed at the 15% corporate rate (§ 23 KStG; see de-corporate-tax).

wording: Income that has had wage tax, Kapitalertragsteuer or § 50a tax withheld is settled by the withholding. No return is filed for it. Exceptions where an assessment follows:

section: Step 2: is the tax settled by withholding? (§ 50(2) EStG)
wording: - the person is assessed as fully liable under § 1(3) or § 1a.

section: Step 2: is the tax settled by withholding? (§ 50(2) EStG)
wording: Income with no withholding, such as rent, a German business or a sale of German land, is always assessed.

section: Step 3: the assessment of a non-resident (§ 50(1) EStG)
wording: 1. **Income.** Compute each type as for a resident. Business expenses and Werbungskosten count only if they relate to the German income.

section: Step 3: the assessment of a non-resident (§ 50(1) EStG)
wording: 2. **No personal deductions.** Special expenses, the EUR 36 lump sum, single-parent relief, child allowances, extraordinary burdens and § 35a credits do not apply (§ 50(1) sentence 4). There is no splitting. Exception under § 50(1a): mandatory contributions to a professional pension institution can qualify where membership arises from the admission required for the German professional practice. It covers EU/EEA nationals resident in the EU/EEA or Switzerland, and Swiss nationals resident in the EU or Switzerland. Contributions must directly relate to German income under § 49(1) no. 2 or 3 from that admitted practice; the deduction follows German qualifying income divided by the total positive German and foreign income from that practice. It is excluded to the extent already deducted in the residence state or exceeding the German qualifying income.
evidence_note: DE-L13 source correction: actual50(1a) mandatory-professional-pension exception is quoted with own gates/allocation; no blanket exclusion is certified.

section: Step 3: the assessment of a non-resident (§ 50(1) EStG)
wording: 3. **Employees are the exception.** For employment income under § 49(1) no. 4, pension and health insurance contributions and the EUR 36 lump sum are allowed, for the period of the German employment and up to that employment income (§ 50(1) sentence 5). The employee lump sum (EUR 1,230, § 9a) is a Werbungskosten lump sum and applies anyway; it and the EUR 36 are cut pro rata for part-year work (§ 50(1) sentence 6).

section: Step 3: the assessment of a non-resident (§ 50(1) EStG)
wording: 4. **Grundfreibetrag added back.** Apply the tariff to taxable income plus EUR 12,348. For employment income, add only the part of EUR 12,348 above the employment income less allowed deductions. In effect a non-resident employee keeps the allowance on wages; a landlord or business owner does not.

section: Step 3: the assessment of a non-resident (§ 50(1) EStG)
wording: 5. **Solidarity surcharge** at 5.5% of the income tax, with the same EUR 20,350 threshold as residents.

section: Step 4: the § 1(3) assessment instead
wording: The person is taxed as a resident on their German income: Grundfreibetrag, special expenses, the EUR 36 lump sum and the resident deductions apply. Income that is not subject to German tax is left out of the base but raises the rate (progression, § 32b(1) no. 5 EStG): the tax rate is found on taxable income plus that foreign income, then applied to taxable income alone. Splitting needs § 1a. Foreign capital income is a special case: § 2(5b) EStG keeps capital income under § 32d(1) out of "income" wherever the law refers to it, and whether foreign interest or dividends of a § 1(3) applicant count in the 90% test and in the progression is not settled here (see Not yet confirmed).

section: Wage tax for non-resident employees
wording: - Non-resident employees are in tax class I (§ 38b(1) no. 1(b) EStG), unless treated as fully liable under § 1(3) or § 1a.

section: Wage tax for non-resident employees
wording: - The employer's Betriebsstättenfinanzamt (the tax office for the place of business), not a residence office, sets and changes their wage tax data and issues the tax ID (§ 39(2) sentence 2 and § 39(3) EStG).

section: Wage tax for non-resident employees
wording: - A § 1(3) or § 1a employee with wage tax data set this way must file (§ 46(2) no. 7(b) EStG). An employee who wants § 1(3) treatment only in the assessment applies with a return (§ 46(2) no. 9), at the employer's Betriebsstättenfinanzamt.

section: § 50a withholding (artists, athletes, royalties, supervisory boards)
wording: - The German payer withholds when the payment is made: 15% of gross, 30% for supervisory board fees, plus 5.5% surcharge on the tax. Travel and hotel costs the payer refunds count as receipts only above actual cost and the per diem lump sums.

section: § 50a withholding (artists, athletes, royalties, supervisory boards)
wording: - For § 50a(1) nos. 1, 2 and 4 only, the payer may deduct directly related costs proved in a form the BZSt can check or paid by the payer, then withhold 30% for an EU/EEA national resident in the EU/EEA, or 15% for a company meeting § 32(4) KStG. This net route does not apply to royalties under § 50a(1) no. 3 (§ 50a(3)).
evidence_note: DE-L12 source correction: NET applies only50a(1)1/2/4, not royalty3; actual nationality/residence and corporate conditions must be established.

section: § 50a withholding (artists, athletes, royalties, supervisory boards)
wording: - The payer files the withholding return with the BZSt by the 10th of the month after each calendar quarter and pays it over (§ 50a(5)). It must file even when nothing is withheld. The payer is liable for tax not withheld; the creditor can also be pursued.

section: § 50a withholding (artists, athletes, royalties, supervisory boards)
wording: - On request the payer issues a certificate of the tax withheld (§ 50a(5) sentence 7). The creditor needs it for a refund.

section: Treaty relief: exemption and refund (§ 50c EStG)
wording: - The payer withholds in full even when a treaty limits German tax, unless the creditor holds an exemption certificate (Freistellungsbescheinigung) from the BZSt (§ 50c(1), (2)). For dividends, a treaty exemption certificate is given only to a company holding at least 10% of a German company.

section: Treaty relief: exemption and refund (§ 50c EStG)
wording: - Small royalties: where a treaty bars German tax and the year's royalties from that payer stay at or below EUR 10,000, the payer need not withhold (§ 50c(2) no. 2), but must still file the withholding return.

section: Treaty relief: exemption and refund (§ 50c EStG)
wording: - Refund: the creditor applies to the BZSt, electronically, within four years from the end of the year of receipt, with a residence certificate from their own tax authority and the payer's tax certificate (§ 50c(3), (5)). The BZSt warns that refunds can take more than 20 months.

section: Treaty relief: exemption and refund (§ 50c EStG)
wording: - Companies: treaty relief is denied to an interposed company whose owners would not get it directly and which has no real business of its own (§ 50d(3) EStG).
evidence_note: Actual50d(3) sentence2 purpose/listed-company escape is preserved in quote; current short main-rule description is not a complete treaty-shopping adjudication.

section: Kapitalertragsteuer on dividends to non-residents
wording: The German company withholds 25% plus 5.5% surcharge, 26.375% in all, whoever the shareholder is. For a non-resident shareholder without a German business, that settles the German tax. The excess over the treaty rate is reclaimed from the BZSt under § 50c(3). Example: a treaty limit of 15% gives a refund of 26.375% − 15% = 11.375% of the gross dividend. A foreign company that cannot use a treaty still gets two fifths of the tax back (§ 44a(9)). The treaty rate itself depends on the treaty; see de-treaty-withholding-rates for the rates by country.

section: Foreign tax credit for residents (§ 34c and § 32d(5) EStG)
wording: Which rule applies depends on the income:

section: Foreign tax credit for residents (§ 34c and § 32d(5) EStG)
wording: - **Capital income under the flat tax (§ 32d(1)), such as foreign dividends and interest of a private investor.** § 34c does not apply (§ 34c(1) sentence 1, second half). The foreign tax is credited under § 32d(5): at most 25% of each item, and at most the German tax on the capital income. The flat tax is then (e − 4q) / 4 without church tax, where e is the capital income after the Sparer-Pauschbetrag and q the creditable foreign tax (§ 32d(1) sentence 4). Income that had no German Kapitalertragsteuer, for example through a foreign broker, is declared in the return (§ 32d(3)).

section: Foreign tax credit for residents (§ 34c and § 32d(5) EStG)
wording: - **Other foreign income taxed at the tariff (for example foreign rent, foreign business income).** § 34c(1) applies where no treaty exists; where a treaty provides for a credit, § 34c(6) applies the same method. Capital income assessed under the § 32d(6) Günstigerprüfung instead keeps the § 32d(5) credit, capped at the additional tariff tax on that capital income (§ 32d(6) sentence 2). For income within § 34c, the foreign tax is credited up to the German tax on that income:
evidence_note: DE-L11 source correction:32d(6) keeps32d(5), excludes34c; foreign tax is reduced by actual refund entitlement before the German cap.

section: Foreign tax credit for residents (§ 34c and § 32d(5) EStG)
wording: credit cap = German tariff tax × foreign income from that country / taxable income (sentence 2: the average rate on the whole taxable income, applied to the foreign income).

section: Foreign tax credit for residents (§ 34c and § 32d(5) EStG)
wording: Foreign tax above the cap is lost. Only tax that was set, paid and reduced by any refund due abroad counts. Instead of the credit the taxpayer can deduct the foreign tax from the income (§ 34c(2)).

section: Foreign tax credit for residents (§ 34c and § 32d(5) EStG)
wording: - **Income a treaty exempts in Germany** (often foreign employment income or foreign rent): no credit, but it raises the rate under § 32b(1) no. 3. Exception: rent from property in another EU/EEA state, and profits of an EU/EEA permanent establishment that fails the active-business test of § 2a(2), do not raise the rate (§ 32b(1) sentence 2).

section: Foreign tax credit for residents (§ 34c and § 32d(5) EStG)
wording: What counts as foreign income is set out in § 34d EStG.

section: Penalties and interest
wording: - **Late filing surcharge (§ 152 AO).** 0.25% per started month of the tax less prepayments and withholding, at least EUR 25 per month, at most EUR 25,000. It is compulsory if the return is not filed within 14 months after the end of the year (for 2026: by 29 February 2028), unless an extension was granted, the tax is nil or negative, or the tax does not exceed prepayments and withholding (§ 152(2), (3) AO).

section: Penalties and interest
wording: - **Interest (§ 233a, § 238 AO).** 0.15% per full month (1.8% a year) on the balance, from 15 months after year end: from 1 April 2028 for 2026.

section: Penalties and interest
wording: - **Late payment (§ 240 AO).** 1% per started month on the overdue tax rounded down to EUR 50.

section: Penalties and interest
wording: - **§ 50a payer.** The payer is liable for tax it did not withhold or pay over (§ 50a(5) sentence 5). The creditor can also be pursued.

section: Cross-border points
wording: - **Treaties override.** A treaty can take away Germany's right to tax (for example employment income under the 183-day rule) or cap it (dividends, royalties). Withholding still happens first; relief is by exemption certificate or refund (§ 50c).
evidence_note: The183-day statement is a generic treaty illustration/referral, not an established result under an identified treaty. Full employer/PE and reference-period conditions are not supplied here.

section: Cross-border points
wording: - **Moving in or out during the year.** A person who is fully liable for part of the year is assessed once; foreign income of the non-resident months raises the rate (§ 2(7), § 32b(1) no. 2 EStG). Not set out further here.

section: Cross-border points
wording: - **Leaving with shares.** See leaving-germany-exit-tax, including extended limited liability under § 2 AStG after a move to a low-tax country.

section: Cross-border points
wording: - **VAT.** A non-resident letting German property or performing in Germany may also have German VAT duties. Not covered here; see germany-vat-return.

section: Cross-border points
wording: - **Church tax.** Not dealt with here; it is set by state law.

section: Example 1: Austrian resident with a German rental flat
wording: Anna lives in Vienna and has no home in Germany. Her German flat produces a rental result of EUR 24,000 for 2026, computed as in de-rental-income. Her only other income is a rental result of EUR 2,000 from a garage she lets in Vienna. (Invented case.)

section: Example 1: Austrian resident with a German rental flat
wording: **Limited liability (default).** No personal deductions, no EUR 36 lump sum. Taxable income EUR 24,000. The tariff is applied to 24,000 + 12,348 = 36,348. z = (36,348 − 17,799) / 10,000 = 1.8549. Tax = (173.10 × 1.8549 + 2,397) × 1.8549 + 1,034.87 = 6,076.65, rounded down EUR 6,076. Below EUR 20,350, so no surcharge.
evidence_note: Guide expressly reserves progression-rate rounding and uses unrounded fraction in executable fixture. Actual2025 handbook truncation in partners ledger is not silently transplanted as a verified2026 assessment instruction.

section: Example 1: Austrian resident with a German rental flat
wording: **§ 1(3) option.** German income is 24,000 / 26,000 = 92.3% of her total, and the Austrian income is under EUR 12,348 (Austria is in country group 1), so both tests pass. She needs a certificate from the Austrian tax office for the EUR 2,000. Taxable income 24,000 − 36 = EUR 23,964. The Austrian rent is not subject to German tax, so it raises the rate (§ 32b(1) no. 5; the EU/EEA rent exception in § 32b(1) sentence 2 covers only no. 3): tax on 23,964 + 2,000 = 25,964 is EUR 3,107, a rate of 11.9666%. Tax = 23,964 × 11.9666% = EUR 2,867. The option saves EUR 3,209.

wording: Jan lives in Munich. In 2026 he receives EUR 10,000 of dividends from a foreign company through a foreign broker. The source country withheld 15% (EUR 1,500), its treaty rate. He has no other capital income and is not a church member. (Invented case.)

section: Example 2: German resident with foreign dividends taxed 15% abroad
wording: **Which regime.** These are private capital income under § 32d(1) EStG, so § 34c does not apply (§ 34c(1) sentence 1, second half, and § 34c(6) sentence 2). The credit is under § 32d(5). Because no German bank withheld, he declares the dividends in the return (§ 32d(3)).

section: Example 2: German resident with foreign dividends taxed 15% abroad
wording: - Cap 1: 25% of the dividend, EUR 2,500. Cap 2: the German tax on the capital income, EUR 2,250. The EUR 1,500 paid is under both, so q = EUR 1,500 is credited in full.

section: Example 2: German resident with foreign dividends taxed 15% abroad
wording: If he had chosen the tariff under § 32d(6), § 32d(5) still governs the credit, applied to the additional tariff tax on the capital income. The foreign tax must first be reduced by any source-country refund entitlement. If 30% (EUR 3,000) were withheld but the same treaty limits source tax to 15%, only EUR 1,500 is creditable in this case and EUR 1,500 is reclaimed from the source country; the German tax cap does not turn treaty-refundable tax into a German credit. In a separate no-refund-entitlement case with EUR 3,000 of eligible foreign tax, the German cap would limit credit to EUR 2,250 and EUR 750 would remain uncredited.
